stages.name: Orientation
stages.blurb: What AI is, where it came from, why it matters.

stages.name: Math you actually need
stages.blurb: Just enough linear algebra, calculus and probability.

stages.name: Learning from data
stages.blurb: Classic ML, then neural networks from scratch.

stages.name: Deep learning
stages.blurb: Making deep nets train, and the models that see and sequence.

stages.name: Transformers & LLMs
stages.blurb: Attention, then how large language models really work.

stages.name: Frontier
stages.blurb: Post-training, systems, building with LLMs, safety.

stages.name: Electives
stages.blurb: Reinforcement learning, generative models, AI in the world.

nodes.name: The big picture
nodes.desc: History of AI, what models can and cannot do, impact on work and society, expert overviews of the field.

nodes.name: Linear algebra
nodes.desc: Vectors, matrices, linear maps, eigenvectors, dot products as similarity.

nodes.name: Calculus & gradients
nodes.desc: Derivatives, chain rule, gradients, optimization intuition.

nodes.name: Probability & information
nodes.desc: Probability, Bayes, statistics, entropy and information theory.

nodes.name: Machine learning foundations
nodes.desc: Supervised learning, regression, classification, overfitting, classic ML algorithms, intro ML courses.

nodes.name: Neural networks & backprop
nodes.desc: Neurons, layers, loss, backpropagation, building a net from scratch.

nodes.name: Training deep nets
nodes.desc: Optimizers, initialization, normalization, regularization, debugging training.

nodes.name: CNNs & computer vision
nodes.desc: Convolutions, image models, detection, vision transformers, speech and perception.

nodes.name: Language modeling & embeddings
nodes.desc: Character/word models, embeddings, RNNs, LSTMs, classic NLP.

nodes.name: Attention & transformers
nodes.desc: Self-attention, the transformer architecture, building GPT from scratch.

nodes.name: How LLMs work
nodes.desc: Pretraining, tokenization, scaling laws, what happens inside an LLM end to end.

nodes.name: Fine-tuning & RLHF
nodes.desc: Supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, preference optimization, reasoning models trained with RL.

nodes.name: GPUs & efficient AI
nodes.desc: GPU programming, distributed training, inference efficiency, quantization, hardware.

nodes.name: Building with LLMs
nodes.desc: Prompting, RAG, tool use, agents, evals, shipping LLM products.

nodes.name: Safety & interpretability
nodes.desc: Alignment, interpretability, robustness, risks and governance of AI.

nodes.name: Reinforcement learning
nodes.desc: MDPs, policy gradients, Q-learning, AlphaGo-style systems, deep RL courses.

nodes.name: AI in the world
nodes.desc: AI for science, games, robotics, self-driving, ML in production — explained, not just demoed.

videos.t: Vectors | Chapter 1, Essence of linear algebra
videos.o: Understand vectors geometrically as arrows and as lists of numbers, the base of all ML math.
videos.w: HN's go-to recommendation for learning linear algebra intuition, repeatedly credited with making concepts click and complementing textbooks.

q.text: the most welcoming and informative introduction to the topic I've ever seen

videos.t: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd
videos.o: Build a tiny autograd engine in Python and understand exactly how backpropagation trains a neural network.
videos.w: HN treats it as the best starting point for really understanding backprop and neural nets, because Karpathy explains the why with intuition and builds everything in code.

q.text: It's especially useful because he explains the why and provides intuitive explanations instead of just talking about the what and how.

videos.t: But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1
videos.o: Understand what neurons, layers, weights and biases are in a network that recognizes handwritten digits.
videos.w: HN treats it as the standard first stop for learning neural networks, praised for making the math intuitive.

q.text: the visualisations and explanations of the math/concepts are so amazing

videos.t: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.
videos.o: Build a small GPT in PyTorch from scratch, implementing self-attention and the transformer block yourself.
videos.w: It is the go-to recommendation for learning how transformers and LLMs actually work, praised for its clarity and Karpathy's teaching.

q.text: the best video I have seen on the topic

videos.t: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs | Deep Learning Chapter 5
videos.o: Follow data through a GPT-style transformer: tokens, embeddings, attention and next-token prediction, shown visually.
videos.w: HN treats it as the go-to visual introduction to transformers, and many say it finally made attention and embeddings click.

q.text: what bade me finally understand the transformer architecture [0] and attention [1], are 3Blue1Brown's videos.

videos.t: Lec 1 | MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra, Spring 2005
videos.o: See linear equations geometrically as rows and columns, the starting point of Strang's full linear algebra course.
videos.w: It is HN's default recommendation for learning linear algebra, praised for Strang's teaching and for building real understanding useful in machine learning.

q.text: I highly recommend the MIT 18.06 open course on linear algebra - the lectures are first rate.

videos.t: What Happened to Horses Is Happening to Us
videos.o: The 2014 case that automation could make much human labor economically obsolete, as engines did horses.
videos.w: HN has recommended it for a decade as the standard explainer on automation and unemployment, though skeptics later cite it as an example of overconfident predictions.

q.text: Excellent video on the subject: CGPGrey - Humans Need Not Apply

videos.t: MarI/O - Machine Learning for Video Games
videos.o: Grasp how neuroevolution (NEAT) evolves neural networks that learn to play Super Mario World.
videos.w: The go-to accessible introduction to neuroevolution and NEAT, praised for crediting prior research.

q.text: his brief videos give a really nice introduction to the topic that should be accessible to most people

videos.t: AlphaGo - The Movie | Full award-winning documentary
videos.o: See how AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in 2016 and why that match became an AI milestone.
videos.w: HN commenters call it a moving, well-made human story about AI and Go that works for non-technical viewers and does not date.

q.text: I consider AlphaGo - The Movie [1] to be a timeless classic that will never feel outdated.

videos.t: Let's build the GPT Tokenizer
videos.o: Build a byte pair encoding tokenizer from scratch and trace odd LLM behaviors back to tokenization.
videos.w: Recommended as the best deep dive on tokenizers, worth the two hours for anyone working with LLMs.

q.text: Worth spending 2h for the deeper understanding if you deal with LLMs.

videos.t: RL Course by David Silver - Lecture 1: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
videos.o: Learn the core vocabulary of reinforcement learning: agents, rewards, states, policies, value functions and models.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as an excellent, clear introductory RL course from the lead of AlphaGo, pairing well with Sutton and Barto.

q.text: Really clear explanations that went hand in hand when I was reading Sutton and Barto's introductory book.

videos.t: Lecture 1 | Machine Learning (Stanford)
videos.o: Get an overview of supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning as framed in Stanford CS229.
videos.w: Recommended as the rigorous, math-heavy original course, deeper than the Coursera version, for learning machine learning.

q.text: I'd suggest going back to the original youtube[1] and course materials[2].

videos.t: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
videos.o: Understand how ChatGPT-style models are built end to end, from pretraining data to post-training, and why they hallucinate.
videos.w: HN's most frequent recommendation for a clear, approachable foundation in how LLMs work without heavy math.

q.text: I highly recommend Andrej Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT

videos.t: Computer program that learns to play classic NES games
videos.o: How a program infers a game's objective from memory patterns and searches inputs to play NES games.
videos.w: Loved on HN as a hilarious, brilliant example of hacker-academic work and cited whenever game-playing AI or fuzzing comes up.

q.text: Watch the whole thing, it's delightful.

videos.t: The essence of calculus
videos.o: See where derivatives, integrals and the fundamental theorem of calculus come from geometrically.
videos.w: A staple recommendation for anyone learning math, praised for visual intuition that makes memorized formulas make sense.

q.text: When I discovered that video, all the formulas they tried to make me memorize started making a LOT more sense.

videos.t: Bay Area Vision Meeting: Unsupervised Feature Learning and Deep Learning
videos.o: Understand the early deep learning idea of learning features from unlabeled data instead of hand-designing them.
videos.w: HN commenters recommended it for years as a simple, exciting overview of the deep learning wave.

q.text: he explains very simply how all this works for images and some examples about the audio case.

videos.t: A Hackers' Guide to Language Models
videos.o: Use language models in code: call the API, test capabilities and limits, and fine-tune an open model.
videos.w: Repeatedly named the best practical tutorial for using LLMs, with a well-liked fine-tuning section.

q.text: highly recommend "Hackers Guide to language models" by Jeremy Howard. 1.5h video packed with practical information

videos.t: Andrej Karpathy - AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla
videos.o: Learn how Tesla trains vision neural nets on fleet data to replace hand-written driving code.
videos.w: HN repeatedly points to it as the best public technical overview of Tesla's FSD approach, used both to defend and to critique Tesla's progress.

q.text: I highly recommend watching head of AI at Tesla Andrej Karpathy's talk on their self driving architecture.

videos.t: The determinant | Chapter 6, Essence of linear algebra
videos.o: Understand the determinant as how much a linear transformation scales area or volume.
videos.w: HN repeatedly points people to it as the clearest visual intuition for determinants, often saying it finally made the concept click.

q.text: I have warmed up to determinants ever since I saw 3Blue1Brown give a fairly intuitive explanation for them

videos.t: Why Would AI Want to do Bad Things? Instrumental Convergence
videos.o: Understand instrumental convergence: why agents with almost any goal seek resources and self-preservation.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as the clearest introduction to why smart AI might behave badly by default.

q.text: Robert Miles' videos are among the best presented arguments about specific points in this list

videos.t: [1hr Talk] Intro to Large Language Models
videos.o: Get a clear mental model of what LLMs are, how they are trained, and their security weaknesses.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the dense, approachable starting point for understanding LLMs and often cites it for specific claims about scaling and training.

q.text: Start with his short intro to LLMs, only 1 hour long but is dense with valuable stuff

videos.t: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | Chapter 14, Essence of linear algebra
videos.o: Understand what eigenvectors and eigenvalues mean geometrically and why an eigenbasis simplifies a transformation.
videos.w: HN repeatedly names it the best, most intuitive explanation of eigenvalues, and a gateway to the whole linear algebra series.

q.text: By far the best explanation of eigenvalues is found on 3blue1brown

videos.t: Intelligence and Stupidity: The Orthogonality Thesis
videos.o: Understand why a highly intelligent AI can pursue goals humans find stupid: intelligence and goals are independent.
videos.w: HN people use it as the standard short explanation for why AI can understand human ethics without sharing them, and often recommend the whole channel.

q.text: this video to me states the problem in a nutshell (that whole channel is gold)

videos.t: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD by Martin Görner
videos.o: Build MNIST classifiers from a single layer to convnets and diagnose networks that fail to train.
videos.w: Repeatedly called an excellent, practical introduction that covers a lot in two hours and explains issues academic textbooks skip.

q.text: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD" is really good, and covers a lot of material in a single 2hr talk.

videos.t: Brains, Sex, and Machine Learning
videos.o: Understand dropout as cheap model averaging and why randomness during training reduces overfitting.
videos.w: Recommended as a simple, elegant explanation of dropout and its connection to how the brain works.

q.text: If you want a great overview of the dropout technique, watch this tech talk by Hinton

videos.t: We're building a dystopia just to make people click on ads | Zeynep Tufekci
videos.o: See how engagement-optimizing machine learning shapes what people see and why that concentrates power.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it whenever engagement-optimizing feeds, micro-targeting or ad infrastructure come up, as an accessible warning about algorithmic amplification.

q.text: This TED talk[0] on persuasion architectures brings up some interesting moral arguments against this idea.

videos.t: Robocalypse Now: Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive
videos.o: How Valve trained a deep model on reviewed replays to flag CS:GO cheaters in production.
videos.w: The go-to link in any anti-cheat thread for a concrete, well-delivered account of machine-learning cheat detection in production.

q.text: The presenter delivered the problem and solution approach so well I'd still like to work on something like this some time.

videos.t: Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned — Kenneth Stanley
videos.o: Understand novelty search and open-endedness, and why optimizing fixed objectives can block discovery.
videos.w: Recommended to people who find it inspiring or perspective-changing on pursuing goals, open-ended search and AI beyond optimization.

q.text: It really changed my perspective on achieving my long term goals

videos.t: Lecture 01 - The Learning Problem
videos.o: Understand the learning problem: what it means to learn from data and the main learning types.
videos.w: Recommended repeatedly in 'where do I start with ML' threads as a clear, math-aware introduction.

q.text: I have found the Caltech machine learning intro course to be the most elucidating of any resource so far

videos.t: The spelled-out intro to language modeling: building makemore
videos.o: Build a character-level bigram language model in PyTorch and learn training, sampling and loss.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a long but worthwhile way to demystify how language models work technically.

q.text: It's long (2h), but well worth the time if anyone is curious about the technical workings of LLMs.

videos.t: Future Computers Will Be Radically Different (Analog Computing)
videos.o: Understand why neural network inference is mostly matrix multiplication and how analog chips could do it cheaply.
videos.w: Treated as the accessible reference on analog computing for neural nets, especially the Mythic AI segment.

q.text: Veritasium explains it really well in general here (and demos the device)

videos.t: Intro to AI Safety, Remastered
videos.o: Why advanced AI with misspecified objectives could go wrong, and answers to common objections.
videos.w: The default link for newcomers wanting an approachable, entertaining introduction to AI risk and alignment.

q.text: It's quite an approachable intro, often entertaining

videos.t: Sparks of AGI: early experiments with GPT-4
videos.o: See how researchers probed early GPT-4 across many domains and argued about general intelligence.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a thought-provoking talk from a researcher with early GPT-4 access, especially for the unicorn degrading under safety tuning.

q.text: Highly highly highly recommend listen to this lecture by Sebastien Bubeck

videos.t: Why Not Just: Think of AGI Like a Corporation?
videos.o: Why corporations are a limited analogy for superintelligent AI and what the differences imply for safety.
videos.w: HN points to it as an accessible rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just corporate risk.

q.text: He presents the material in a very interesting and accessible way.

videos.t: Hello World - Machine Learning Recipes #1
videos.o: Train your first supervised classifier with scikit-learn and see what features, labels and training mean.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an approachable first step into machine learning for programmers, with an apples-vs-oranges classifier.

q.text: Very approachable! The first lesson is a classifier to separate apples and oranges.

videos.t: Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep Learning Chapter 6
videos.o: How self-attention, multiple heads and query-key-value matrices let transformers update token meanings.
videos.w: HN treats it as the go-to visual explanation of attention, recommended to people who find text-based transformer explainers hard to follow.

q.text: what bade me finally understand the transformer architecture [0] and attention [1], are 3Blue1Brown's videos.

videos.t: Dasher: information-efficient text entry
videos.o: See how information theory and a predictive language model turn text entry into efficient compression.
videos.w: Regarded as the seminal talk on Dasher, recommended in threads on accessible and alternative text input.

q.text: Dasher is fantastic, because it's based on rock solid information theory, designed by the late David MacKay.

videos.t: GDC 2018: John McDonald (Valve) - Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in CSGO
videos.o: Learn how Valve trained a deep network on reviewed gameplay data to flag cheaters in CS:GO.
videos.w: HN points to it as the definitive example of server-side, behavioral, non-invasive anti-cheat using machine learning, often as a counterpoint to kernel-level anti-cheat.

q.text: The actual presentation is worth listening to if you have the time.

videos.t: LSTM is dead. Long Live Transformers!
videos.o: Understand why RNNs and LSTMs struggle and how multi-head self-attention and positional encoding fix it.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear explanation of why RNNs fall short and how transformers solve it.

q.text: has gotten tons of compliments and keeps people watching year after year

videos.t: Attention Is All You Need
videos.o: Walk through the Attention Is All You Need paper and the original transformer architecture.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible, clear walkthrough of the transformer paper for people with some AI background.

q.text: The Yannic kilcher review is quite good.

videos.t: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule
videos.o: Why accurate tests yield many false positives, and how Bayes factors update odds.
videos.w: HN's go-to link whenever Bayesian reasoning, base rates or imperfect tests come up.

q.text: is a brilliant introduction to the concept

videos.t: The Simple Essence of Automatic Differentiation - Conal Elliott
videos.o: Derive forward and reverse mode automatic differentiation from a simple categorical specification.
videos.w: Cited as the more accessible companion to the paper, and as the most interesting treatment of AD via compiling to categories.

q.text: There's a talk that Conal gives that makes the paper a bit more accessible

videos.t: Backpropagation, intuitively | Deep Learning Chapter 3
videos.o: Build visual intuition for how backpropagation nudges every weight and bias to reduce a network's error.
videos.w: Recommended as the most accessible introduction to backprop for people who struggle with the pure math.

q.text: I found the explainations by 3Brown1Blue to be very intuitive when it comes to neural networks

videos.t: Is AI Safety a Pascal's Mugging?
videos.o: Why the case for AI safety does not rest on tiny probabilities of huge payoffs.
videos.w: HN points to it as a reasoned rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just Pascal's wager.

q.text: the main point of the video is that kind of situation happens when the probability involved is vanishingly small

videos.t: Training AI Without Writing A Reward Function, with Reward Modelling
videos.o: Understand reward modelling: training an AI from human preference comparisons, the core idea behind RLHF.
videos.w: Seen as the clearest introduction to the idea behind RLHF, and also borrowed by commenters as a metaphor for human motivation.

q.text: I find this video by Rob Miles still the best presentation of the ingenious original 2017(!) paper

videos.t: Ali Rahimi's talk at NIPS(NIPS 2017 Test-of-time award presentation)
videos.o: Understand the critique that deep learning practice works without rigorous understanding, and why that matters.
videos.w: HN points to it as the sharpest, most-quoted critique of deep learning practice, and cites it whenever ML reliability or understanding is debated.

q.text: For a more cutting and insightful critique, watch Ali Rahimi's short talk at NIPS 2017

videos.t: How We’re Fooled By Statistics
videos.o: Understand regression to the mean and how ignoring it leads to wrong conclusions from data.
videos.w: HN commenters link it as the clearest short explanation of regression to the mean, especially for how it misleads people about feedback and statistics.

q.text: Veritasium explains it better than me.

videos.t: John Rauser keynote: "Statistics Without the Agonizing Pain" -- Strata + Hadoop 2014
videos.o: Understand p-values and hypothesis testing by simulating and shuffling data instead of using formulas.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an excellent programmer-friendly explanation of p-values and statistical thinking.

q.text: This is an excellent talk I attended a while ago that explains it very well from a programmer's perspective

videos.t: Connections between physics and deep learning
videos.o: Why physical symmetry and locality may explain how small deep networks approximate real-world functions.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clear argument for why deep and cheap learning succeeds, often alongside the associated paper.

q.text: physical data tends to have symmetries, and these symmetries make descriptions of the data very compressible into relatively small neural circuits

videos.t: A visual guide to Bayesian thinking
videos.o: Understand Bayes' rule visually and how priors update with evidence.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a short, accessible intro to Bayesian reasoning and priors.

q.text: The most important mathematical video you will ever see in your life.

videos.t: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2
videos.o: How a neural network learns by minimizing a cost function with gradient descent.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as a very accessible way to understand the math behind machine learning and LLMs.

q.text: 3Blue1Brown which explains math in very accessible way

videos.t: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? - with 'Godfather of AI' Geoffrey Hinton
videos.o: Understand how neural networks learn and why Hinton thinks they may surpass human intelligence.
videos.w: HN readers recommend it as an intuitive explanation of neural networks that shifts how people think about AI and language.

q.text: Richard Sutton takes a different view in an interview with Dwarkesh Patel[2]

videos.t: ai.bythebay.io: George Hotz, Self-Driving Lessons from Comma AI
videos.o: Hear a learning-first argument for self-driving and why the mainstream autonomous-vehicle approach may be flawed.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a candid, contrarian view of self-driving approaches and the real limits of the business.

q.text: George Hotz has a killer talk about why the general approach to autonomous vehicles is flawed. I highly recommend it.

videos.t: Lecture 1: Probability and Counting | Statistics 110
videos.o: Sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, and counting with binomial coefficients.
videos.w: Recommended on Ask HN threads as a high-quality free probability course for relearning math or building an ML foundation.

q.text: I have used and can vouch for the high quality of all of them

videos.t: Lecture 1 | Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning
videos.o: Learn how word vectors work, including skip-gram, CBOW and negative sampling in word2vec.
videos.w: Recommended as one of the best free courses for learning modern deep learning for NLP.

q.text: I will suggest two brilliant courses from Stanford

videos.t: State of GPT | BRK216HFS
videos.o: Understand the GPT assistant pipeline: tokenization, pretraining, supervised finetuning and RLHF, plus prompting tips.
videos.w: Recommended as the clearest overview of how LLM assistants are built and how to use them well.

q.text: It changed the way I use GPT-4.

videos.t: Neural Networks Demystified [Part 1: Data and Architecture]
videos.o: Set up the data and architecture of a simple neural network, first step to coding one in Python.
videos.w: HN commenters point beginners to this series as one of the clearest short walkthroughs of how neural networks and backpropagation work.

q.text: One of the clearest walkthroughs I've seen online is a short series of very short videos by Stephen C Welch [2] [3].

videos.t: Andrej Karpathy: Tesla AI, Self-Driving, Optimus, Aliens, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #333
videos.o: Hear Karpathy explain vision-only self-driving, transformers and where he thinks AI is heading.
videos.w: Cited for Karpathy's first-hand explanations of camera-only self-driving, transformers and ML trends.

q.text: Anyone seriously interested in this question should listen to the Lex Friedman interview of Andrej Karpathy

videos.t: Do we need Attention? - Linear RNNs and State Space Models (SSMs) for NLP
videos.o: How linear RNNs and state space models work as alternatives to attention for long sequences.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for building intuition about state space models and the tradeoffs between transformer and SSM layers.

q.text: I highly recommend Sasha Rush's video on it

videos.t: [CVPR'21 WAD] Keynote - Andrej Karpathy, Tesla
videos.o: Learn how Tesla built a vision-only driving stack, including depth estimation and large-scale data labeling.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it in Tesla threads as the primary-source explanation of why Tesla removed radar and how its vision depth estimation works.

q.text: This talk was worth watching (any Karpathy or Carmack talk is imo)

videos.t: Google Developers Day US - Theorizing from Data
videos.o: Why large datasets and simple statistical models often beat clever rules in language tasks.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the clear explanation of why Google's statistical, data-first approach works.

q.text: You should definitely watch it if you haven't seen it before.

videos.t: Efficient Bayesian inference with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo -- Michael Betancourt (Part 1)
videos.o: Understand MCMC, why high-dimensional sampling is hard, and the motivation for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
videos.w: HN people return to it as a clear primer on MCMC and HMC and on why high dimensions behave counterintuitively.

q.text: it was a fantastic primer on the basic concepts and motivations of mcmc, and later hmc

videos.t: Peter Norvig - The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data
videos.o: Understand why simple models trained on massive data often beat hand-built models in language tasks.
videos.w: Recommended as a favorite tech talk showing how huge data availability changes how problems are approached.

q.text: Norvig does an especially great job in making you truly appreciate the seismic impact that the availability of massive quantities of data can have

videos.t: Lecture 1: Introduction to Information Theory
videos.o: Learn the core ideas of information theory, entropy and noisy-channel coding from David MacKay.
videos.w: Recommended as an enjoyable, clear introduction to information theory that pairs well with MacKay's free textbook.

q.text: It was very enjoyable for me to learn the material from his lectures.

videos.t: RAAIS 2017 - Simon Knowles, Co-Founder and CTO of Graphcore
videos.c: The Research and Applied AI Summit - RAAIS
videos.o: Why ML chips put memory next to compute, from Graphcore's IPU design rationale.
videos.w: HN points to it as a technical talk from a chip designer on why AI hardware should put memory close to compute and use async data transfers.

q.text: Here's a nice technical talk from Graphcore's CTO about that

videos.t: Jake Vanderplas - Statistics for Hackers - PyCon 2016.mp4
videos.o: Do hypothesis testing with simulation, shuffling and bootstrapping instead of memorized formulas.
videos.w: It is recommended to programmers who want to learn statistics through simulation rather than memorized formulas.

q.text: The presenters advocate using simulation/bootstrapping/shuffling methods instead of memorizing formulas.

videos.t: CS480/680 Lecture 19: Attention and Transformer Networks
videos.o: Understand attention with queries, keys and values, and how transformer networks are assembled.
videos.w: HN recommends it to newcomers as a clear explanation of attention, including the query/key/value intuition.

q.text: I would also recommend Pascal Poupart's talk [1] on Attention and Transformers.

videos.t: 3D Gaussian Splatting! - Computerphile
videos.o: Understand how 3D Gaussian splatting reconstructs a scene from photos and how it compares to NeRF.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible introduction to Gaussian splats, made by people who understand the subject.

q.text: Here's a much better explainer from some people who seem to actually understand the subject matter and not just the buzzwords

videos.t: Dance p 3 Mar09
videos.o: Why p-values vary wildly across replications and why confidence intervals are more informative.
videos.w: Recommended as a vivid visual demonstration of how unreliable p-values are.

q.text: absolutely fantastic and well worth watching

videos.t: Joscha: From Computation to Consciousness (31c3)
videos.o: Explore the computational view of mind that underlies artificial intelligence and cognitive science.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an inspiring summary of a computational model of mind and a first lecture in a series on the brain as a computer.

q.text: stuff like talks by Joscha Bach on C3

videos.t: Large Language Models from scratch
videos.o: Understand language models as learned autocomplete: probabilities, neural networks and gradient descent in plain terms.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a quick, non-dumbed-down way to get up to speed on how LLMs are built.

q.text: I highly recommend this video by Steve Seitz

videos.t: AI Language Models & Transformers - Computerphile
videos.o: Understand how language models generate text and why attention-based transformers beat recurrent networks.
videos.w: Pointed to as an accessible early explanation of transformers and attention for newcomers.

q.text: You can check-out his other videos on NLP as well they are all excellent.

videos.t: Deadly Truth of General AI? - Computerphile
videos.o: See through the stamp-collector thought experiment why a goal-driven general AI need not think like a human.
videos.w: Often pointed to as an accessible first introduction to AI safety and why a superintelligent AI could be dangerous.

q.text: There's a great Computerphile video from 2015 that introduced me to the idea of AI safety awhile ago.

videos.t: Building makemore Part 2: MLP
videos.o: Build an MLP character-level language model with embeddings in PyTorch.

videos.t: Building makemore Part 3: Activations & Gradients, BatchNorm
videos.o: Diagnose activation and gradient statistics, fix initialization, and implement batch normalization by hand.

videos.t: Building makemore Part 4: Becoming a Backprop Ninja

q.text: There's a nice video about this from Numberphile and 3blue1brown

videos.t: Jim Keller - Moore's Law in the age of AI Chips
videos.o: How scalar, vector and GPU-style parallel computation compare for AI chips.
videos.w: Cited in hardware threads as a Keller talk on the different ways of doing parallel processing.

q.text: Jim Keller had an interesting talk recently [1] about ways of doing parallel processing

videos.t: Can we build AI without losing control over it? | Sam Harris
videos.o: Follow the basic argument for why superhuman AI could pose a risk of losing control.
videos.w: HN cites it in AI risk debates, sometimes as an argument that has aged well and sometimes as an example of alarmist framing.

q.text: (Worth a watch if you have 15 mins).

videos.t: Eliezer Yudkowsky: Dangers of AI and the End of Human Civilization | Lex Fridman Podcast #368
videos.o: Understand the strongest pessimistic argument that unaligned superintelligent AI could end human civilization.
videos.w: Mostly cited as the canonical statement of AI doomer views, with some recommending it and many criticizing it as irresponsible or wrong.

q.text: I would recommend listening to Eliezer Yudkowsky on the subject

videos.t: GradIEEEnt half decent: The hidden power of imprecise lines
videos.o: Why networks need nonlinearity, shown by using floating-point rounding as the activation function.
videos.w: Cited as a fun, unconventional example of neural networks built from floating point error.

q.text: A fun example of that (making a neural network using floating point error as a source of non-linearity)

videos.t: Deep Visualization Toolbox
videos.o: See what individual units in a convolutional network respond to, from edges to faces.
videos.w: HN points to it as an intuitive way to see what hidden layers of a convnet learn, and as a reference for hierarchical feature learning.

q.text: Highly recommend this video on the Deep Visualization Toolbox

videos.t: Marcus Hutter: Universal Artificial Intelligence, AIXI, and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #75
videos.o: Understand AIXI, Solomonoff induction and the idea of intelligence as compression.
videos.w: Referenced as an accessible explanation of Kolmogorov complexity and Hutter's view of intelligence as compression.

q.text: it made sense to me

videos.t: How We Prevent the AI’s from Killing us with Paul Christiano
videos.o: Understand the alignment problem and possible solutions from alignment researcher Paul Christiano.
videos.w: HN links it as a balanced, full-length interview with a leading alignment researcher on AI risk.

q.text: Also this whole interview was pretty interesting.

videos.t: Correlation CAN Imply Causation! | Statistics Misconceptions
videos.o: Understand how causal models let you infer causation from correlation in data.
videos.w: HN people link it as a short, accessible summary of Judea Pearl-style causal inference when someone repeats that correlation cannot imply causation.

q.text: A rough summary is available as a YouTube video

videos.t: The Strange Math That Predicts (Almost) Anything
videos.o: Understand Markov chains, how they were discovered, and how they underpin modern prediction algorithms.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an excellent, detailed history of Markov chains, often in threads on Markov models and language models.

q.text: this excellent Veritasium video about Markov and his chains

videos.t: Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again)
videos.o: Karpathy's Software 1.0/2.0/3.0 framing and how to build partial-autonomy LLM apps.
videos.w: HN mostly cites it as a source for Karpathy's framing of programming in English and his generate-then-verify workflow, with a few critics finding it hype.

q.text: I enjoyed Andrej Karpathy's talk about software in the era of AI.

videos.t: Visualizing Data Using t-SNE
videos.o: Learn how t-SNE maps high-dimensional data to 2D and how it compares with other methods.
videos.w: HN people point to it as the canonical explanation from the method's author whenever t-SNE comes up.

q.text: there's a really interesting Google techtalk on how it works

videos.t: Ch(e)at GPT? - Computerphile
videos.o: Understand how biasing token choices watermarks LLM text so it can later be statistically detected.
videos.w: Linked as the approachable explanation whenever HN discusses detecting or watermarking AI-generated text.

q.text: a nice very approachable video explaining it here

videos.t: Did We Just Change Animation Forever?
videos.o: See how fine-tuned Stable Diffusion models turn filmed footage into consistent anime-style video.
videos.w: HN cites it as an example of temporally stable AI video stylization built from ordinary production gear.

q.text: let the results speak for themselves

videos.t: Intelligence is not Enough | Bryan Cantrill | Monktoberfest 2023
videos.o: A skeptical engineer's case that intelligence alone does not make AI an existential threat.
videos.w: Recommended as a thoughtful Cantrill talk on embracing failure and curiosity in engineering, and as a skeptical counterpoint to AI doom narratives.

q.text: I saw Bryan Cantrill's talk on [Intelligence is Not Enough][0]

videos.t: Richard Feynman: Can Machines Think?
videos.o: Feynman's 1985 view on whether machines can think and how to define intelligence.
videos.w: HN uses it as an early authoritative take in debates about AI, reasoning, and AGI.

q.text: It's very difficult to find some way of defining rather precisely something we can do that we can say a computer will never be able to do.

videos.t: But how do AI images and videos actually work? | Guest video by Welch Labs
videos.o: Understand how CLIP embeddings, diffusion sampling and classifier-free guidance produce AI images and video.
videos.w: HN uses it as a clear explainer for diffusion mechanics, such as negative prompts and faster sampling, and for joint text-image encoders.

q.text: WL & 3b1b made a nice video on it

videos.t: Multi-Agent Hide and Seek
videos.o: See how multi-agent self-play produces emergent strategies and tool use without being programmed.
videos.w: HN uses it as a vivid example of emergent behavior from multi-agent reinforcement learning, and as a way to make AI misalignment concerns feel concrete.

q.text: This short video makes the concern much more real

videos.t: Human AI is Decades Away, But We Need to Start the Debate Now | Demis Hassabis | Google Zeitgeist
videos.o: Hear DeepMind's early vision of general AI built through game-playing agents.
videos.w: HN cites it for the DeepMind CEO's early views on AI and its game-playing focus, in AlphaGo and OpenAI threads.

videos.t: Ken Stanley: Discovery Without Objectives
videos.o: Why objective-free novelty search can find solutions that direct optimization misses.
videos.w: Cited as a source for the idea that open-ended search can beat objective-driven optimization, though one commenter found parts of it fluffy.

q.text: I've seen a couple of really interesting talks recently about the surprising successfulness of objective-less search by Ken Stanley

videos.t: Jeff Dean & Noam Shazeer — 25 years at Google: from PageRank to AGI
videos.o: Hear how key Google researchers see the path from PageRank to transformers, mixture of experts and AGI.
videos.w: HN cites it for insight into Google researchers' views on AI progress and publishing, though one commenter finds the interview weak.

q.text: Recommend if you want a taste of what’s Google’s folks take on things.

videos.t: Building the Software 2 0 Stack (Andrej Karpathy)
videos.o: Understand Software 2.0: neural networks trained on curated data replacing hand-written code.
videos.w: HN uses it as the primary source for the 'Software 2.0' idea and recommends it as a quick talk on the next software stack.

q.text: here's a good/quick talk by Andrej Kapathy on what it will take to build the next software stack.

videos.t: We Were Right! Real Inner Misalignment
videos.o: Understand inner misalignment and goal misgeneralization through real RL experiments that demonstrate them.
videos.w: Pointed to as evidence that AI misalignment is an empirically demonstrated problem, for people who dismiss it.

q.text: There have been actual experiments in which AIs appeared to successfully learn their objective in training
